canberra.title: Go Bum! How a cheeky lockdown card game became a book
canberra.snippet: While the rest of us were busy perfecting a sourdough loaf or re-watching The Office for the seventh time during the COVID lockdown, the ...
canberra.content:
Evan Turner is the creative mind behind the story in The Bumlings, a book inspired by a card game his son created. Photo: Supplied.

While the rest of us were busy perfecting a sourdough loaf or re-watching The Office for the seventh time during the COVID lockdown, the Evans family was creating Go Bum.

It started as a cheeky version of the classic Go Fish card game. In the game, created by Evan Turner and his then-seven-year-old son Levi, players match bums of everything from robots to cats.

Go Bum quickly hit the shelves of national retailers, before an animal version of the game followed. A myth-inspired edition is set to be released soon.

Six years later, the game is making another transformation, with a book version being released this month.

“I think from the very start we were onto something special, but it’s been a tonne of hard work and quite a few years to get where we are,” Evan told Region.

It was “surreal” when Scholastic Australia reached out to ask if he’d be keen to create a book version of the game.

It took about 18 months to create the book, whose story follows a search effort after Teeny Tiny Bum goes missing.

“I never saw myself as an author, but it’s something that I’ve really enjoyed.

“I’m a pretty creative person and getting to expand the game to a whole world, filled with characters and coming up with stories, has been a really fun experience.”

Evan described keeping to the word limit for a children’s book as being “surprisingly tricky”.

“When you’re trying to get lots of fun jokes in there, it can be really tricky. Every word counts.

“I definitely got lots of input from my wife and kids. My wife actually got a nice joke in there – that made it into the final cut.”

To bring the game to life on paper, Evan partnered with Netherlands-based illustrator Dewy Venerius.

He says he was “thrilled” at the prospect of creating new designs to go with the original game’s 25 different bums.

“She turned our illustrations [from the game] into the wonderful illustrations that you see.”

The book is available online and in physical stores. Photo: Supplied.

Evan is hopeful that the book sparks an interest in reading among kids, pointing to the works of “great Australian authors” like Andy Griffiths and Aaron Blabey that inspired him.

“If we can do something similar with The Bumlings, I would just be ecstatic at the idea of kids getting into reading from something I’ve done.”

About six years on from the initial release of Go Bum, Evan is excited for other families to read – and enjoy – the book version.

“I think it’s a little bit surprising but also a little bit not,” he said of the game’s success.

“When I first sat down with Levi, and we played the first game of Go Bum together, it was all very hand-drawn and very homemade. But when he said, ‘Dad, do you have stinky bum?’ … I could just see the possibilities opening up.”

After all, while there are some jokes in the book for parents, the focus is on getting youngsters to grin.

“I think kids love books where they are fully engaged. I think what’s most important is that they’re enjoying the process,” he says.

“I really hope that The Bumlings is one of those books where parents or grandparents and their young ones can laugh together.”

The Bumlings is available for purchase from September from physical and online retailers, as well as Scholastic Book Club and Scholastic Book Fairs. A book launch will be held at Harry Hartog Tuggeranong (in the South.Point Shopping Centre) later this month.

canberra.title: Too young for a diagnosis, too difficult for childcare: Where do families turn?
canberra.snippet: When a Canberra mother was told her four-year-old son could no longer attend his childcare centre, she did what many parents would: she l...
canberra.content:
What happens when a young child clearly needs additional support but the childcare centre isn’t able to provide it? Photo: Supplied.

When a Canberra mother was told her four-year-old son could no longer attend his childcare centre, she did what many parents would: she looked for help. She complained to multiple bodies, hoping someone could help resolve the dispute or find a way forward.

But despite exploring every avenue, she couldn’t find a solution. Her son Sam* was ultimately removed from care.

Behind the family’s experience is a much bigger question: what happens when a young child clearly needs additional support, but a mainstream childcare centre says it can no longer safely provide it?

Sam had been displaying increasingly challenging behaviour and was participating in an Inclusion Support Program.

His family sought professional help and explored whether he could have ADHD, but were told he was too young for a formal diagnosis.

A cognitive assessment instead found he had a Full Scale IQ of 132, placing him in the “very superior” range. His psychologist indicated he may be twice-exceptional – gifted while also having a developmental difference – although further assessment would have to wait until he was older.

His mother says she expected that information to lead to more support.

Instead, days later, she was called to a meeting and told Sam had been identified as a “safety concern”. His attendance would be restricted to a maximum of six hours a day.

She says she received only three working days’ notice of the change.

His care was subsequently ended altogether.

The child care centre said the decision was not based on a diagnosis – actual or potential – but continuing concerns about the safety of other children and educators.

“We worked with the family over time and put additional supports in place, including an individual inclusion plan and adjusted attendance hours to maximise educator support,” a spokesperson told Region.

“Despite these measures, there were ongoing safety concerns for other children and educators.”

The centre said it supports hundreds of children with additional needs, including ADHD and autism, using behaviour plans, changes to environments and programming and additional educator strategies.

So when a child is kicking, spitting or becoming verbally aggressive, what should a centre actually do?

Senior clinical psychologist from Strategic Psychology Nesh Nikolic, who has not assessed Sam and could not comment on his individual case, said the first mistake was assuming difficult behaviour had one obvious cause.

It could involve biological, social or environmental factors, sensory issues or even a mismatch between a child’s intellectual ability and the activities they are being given.

“Usually it’s several at once interacting,” he said.

For a gifted or potentially twice-exceptional child, something as ordinary as a noisy room, unpredictable routine or activities that are not stimulating enough could contribute to escalating behaviour.

“A child who is intellectually well ahead of the activities on offer, and who is still four, will often show us that mismatch behaviourally rather than tell us about it,” Mr Nikolic said.

“Add sensory load and unpredictability, and you have a reasonable recipe for escalation.”

The solutions do not necessarily need to be complicated.

Predictable routines, warning a child before transitions, providing a quiet space before they become overwhelmed, making activities more challenging and having a consistent educator working with the child can all help.

“None of that is exotic, but it does require someone to plan it and everyone to do it the same way,” Mr Nikolic said.

But understanding why a child behaves a certain way does not mean a centre should tolerate unsafe behaviour.

“Knowing why a behaviour is happening doesn’t make it safe in the moment,” he said.

“You can hold both: a compassionate formulation of the child, and a firm, immediate response to keep everyone safe. Understanding is not permission.”

There can also be a point where a mainstream centre simply cannot provide the level of individual attention a child needs.

Educators repeatedly being kicked, hit or abused cannot be expected to simply accept it as part of their job.

“Protecting them isn’t in competition with inclusion, it’s a precondition for it,” Mr Nikolic said.

The bigger problem, he believes, is often how families and centres reach that point – and what happens next.

Instead of waiting until the relationship reaches crisis point, centres and families should have a written plan early, documenting what triggers behaviour, what strategies are being tried and whether they are working.

There should be regular reviews, one consistent point of contact for the family, early specialist involvement and, crucially, an agreed plan for what happens if the centre eventually cannot cope.

“If everyone knows from the start what the limits are and what the next step would be, nobody is blindsided when it comes,” Mr Nikolic said.

But there is another gap that is much harder for an individual centre or parent to fix. Young children can have obvious additional needs while being too young for the diagnosis that can unlock formal support.

“The pre-diagnosis window is the genuinely hard part,” Mr Nikolic said.

He believes support should respond to a child’s demonstrated needs rather than depend solely on a diagnostic code. And when a centre genuinely cannot continue care, simply showing the family the door should not be the end of the process.

A better system, Mr Nikolic said, would help move the child towards a setting that can meet their needs through a planned transition.

“A fair outcome, to my mind, is one where the child doesn’t lose access to care and connection altogether but is moved toward a setting that can actually meet him, with a planned transition rather than a cliff edge,” he said.

*Names have been changed to protect the family’s identity.

canberra.title: A visit to Villaggio Sant’ Antonio’s Little Italy yields benefits beyond a good brew
canberra.snippet: A little golden caravan is acting as a beacon for Page residents, attracting anyone seeking connection, conversation and a good brew. Mum...
canberra.content:
Of Italian descent herself, Villaggio Sant’ Antonio CEO Giulia Jones is bringing the vitality of village life to Page – connecting young and old. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

A little golden caravan is acting as a beacon for Page residents, attracting anyone seeking connection, conversation and a good brew.

Mums and bubs, remote workers, and of course, the elderly residents of the Villaggio Sant’ Antonio retirement community all converge at this slow-paced coffee shop, where lingering in line or joining a neighbouring table is encouraged.

The Little Italy Village Cafe is a community-building initiative of Villaggio Sant’ Antonio.

It’s also Page’s only cafe – making it an immediate hit, with over 400 coffees brewed at its launch earlier this month.

The space is the first to join the Foundation for Social Health’s Third Spaces Network, which aims to tackle loneliness by supporting everyday places for social connection.

Nurturing a village mentality and incidental socialising was very much core to the project, according to Villaggio Sant’ Antonio CEO Giulia Jones.

“The solution to loneliness can be as simple as a 10-minute conversation once a week,” she says.

“It’s actually hugely important to human satisfaction and meaning. You want to be noticed, and you want to be seen.”

And loneliness is not limited by age.

Last year, a University of Canberra study of the ACT Region found that nearly 19 per cent of respondents aged 30 to 49 years old said they often or always feel lonely.

“The blue zones around the world – where people live the longest and report the most satisfying lives – are places where there’s meaningful, incidental intergenerational connection,” says Giulia.

Visiting Little Italy, I find a diverse gathering of young and old – all of whom are keen to say hello.

I met Maggie in line for coffee. She’s energised, arriving with her yoga group, ready to settle in a sun-drenched spot.

Later, Katie swings past our table – she’s the Villa Manager and one of the “real movers” behind the van.

Behind her, Jenny the Villa Committee President pops her head in, but can’t stay today – seemingly, she’s on a mission.

I’m even lucky enough to meet Jake, working his first shift in the van supported through the NDIS. This social enterprise seems like the perfect place for him to flex his already impressive customer service skills.

There’s a comfortable sense of hustle and bustle here, though no one is really in a hurry.

Photo: Supplied.

Professional Baristas make the brews, friendly faces man the register, and Chef Gerhan supplies the treats. Photo: Supplied.

Photo: Supplied.

Photo: Supplied.

Photo: Supplied.

Founder of the project, CEO Giulia Jones added plenty of personal touches to its creation, including her own Saint Anthony of Padua medallion.

“One of the beautiful things about aged-care is everything is slow,” says Giulia.

“This is a slow-living cafe. There’s no rush. It’s not like most coffee shops. There’s plenty of chairs and tables, and we’re not that commercial that we have to push you out.

“We want people to come and just sit there for as long as they need.”

Over coffee, I sit in conversation with Page resident, Lena Azzapardi – and this is where I feel the impact of the space.

I learn that Lena and her husband Joe left Malta in 1971, arriving on Australian shores with a 12-month-old baby, two pieces of luggage and £100.

She says life in Malta was beautiful, but difficult.

After the death of Joe’s mother, the couple moved into the family home to care for his father and Joe’s brother with Down syndrome. Together, they would walk down the road for a daily swim, or grab a basket to visit the markets, chatting to neighbours along the way.

“I lived there with him for three years, but I couldn’t continue to do it because I was feeding three men on £2 a week!”

Five decades later, Lena now rises early each morning to meet Joe in the dementia ward, where he has been for six months.

Sometimes they walk past the self-contained villas, where Lena says she’s made friends with many residents.

“When you go past, you get about 6 million hellos,” she says.

Occasionally, Joe wants to go to the mall – though that’s a more challenging outing.

Little Italy gives Lena and Joe a new accessible option on their doorstep.

The café also keeps isolation at bay for those who don’t have loved ones dropping by.

“In a facility like this, there’s always about 20 per cent of residents who have zero visitors,” says Giulia.

That’s why every morning around 9 am, the Wellbeing Team chauffeurs residents to Little Italy.

But how do they facilitate this culture for connection?

As a former ACT MLA, Giulia says it’s all in the messaging – and her political skills came in handy in getting the word out.

“All of our advertising is about social connection, so people actually come in here with that in mind.

“I was here last Saturday and noticed a resident and someone from the next door retirement village sitting together at a table. When a young mum came along, one of the residents said ‘Don’t sit by yourself. Come and sit with us’.

“That’s it. That’s the goal. Once you’ve got that happening, you’ve got real connection.”

For me, my 10-minute conversation with Lena changed my whole week.

As a busy Mum and remote worker, I found it surprisingly refreshing to meet someone new in this social space engineered specifically for connection.

And that’s why I’m planning my trip back to Little Italy.

The Little Italy Village Cafe is located at 35 Burkitt Street, Page. It’s open from 7 am to 11 am, seven days a week.

canberra.title: Handball prodigy turns freak injury into new opportunity with sights set on Brisbane 2032
canberra.snippet: Handball is a relatively unknown sport in Australia, but for Canberran Brianna Keyes, it’s one she’s played for over half her...
canberra.content:
Brianna Keyes has been playing handball for over 15 years, but after a freak accident, she has continued her sporting career in the wheelchair version of the game. Photo: Supplied.

Handball is a relatively unknown sport in Australia, but for Canberran Brianna Keyes, it’s one she’s played for over half her life as both an able-bodied and a wheelchair athlete.

Having played the sport at the highest levels for over a decade, Brianna travelled the world and competed against some of the sport’s juggernauts. But when a freak ankle injury and a botched surgery meant she could no longer compete, it looked like all was said and done on her playing career.

Fortunately, there was another way Brianna could continue playing the sport she loved. Only this time, it involved wheelchairs.

With the Brisbane 2032 Paralympics just around the corner, she’s now helping push the sport here in Australia in an effort to have wheelchair handball officially included in the 2032 Brisbane Paralympics.

“I started playing handball when I was 16. We had some scouts come to a gala day at our school because the sport isn’t huge here. The scouts gave me a letter asking if I would be interested in trying out,” Brianna said.

“I was a state-level basketball player at the time, but I said I’d give it a go and quickly fell in love with it, going through all the ranks and eventually playing in the Youth Olympics in 2010.

“From there, I played full-time for the next 10 years or so, travelling the world and having the most incredible experiences.”

On top of the world in many ways, Brianna continued to love handball as much as she ever had. Then a rolled ankle and complications following multiple corrective surgeries on her tendons and ligaments changed everything.

With a weakened ankle that she can barely walk on, Brianna was unable to perform essential athletic movements such as running and jumping, effectively ending any chance of her playing able-bodied handball again.

“I don’t think you kind of realise how amazing that is until it’s kind of taken away,” she said.

“I just stepped on someone’s foot while playing and did a really good job hurting it. It sustained quite heavy trauma and required several corrective surgeries, which ended up only making things worse and left me with a permanent disability.

“I went from being at the pinnacle of handball, getting ready to head to the world championships, to not being able to stand for long periods of time.”

Brianna in full flight at the 2019 World Championships in Japan. Photo: Supplied.

Despite it seeming impossible for her to play handball again, Brianna was introduced to the mixed-gender wheelchair variation of the sport.

Although she is still relatively new to using the chair, her over 15 years of experience has already led to her selection for the world championships in Spain later this month. There she will become the first-ever player to represent their country in both able-bodied and wheelchair competitions.

“It’s relatively new in Australia, and we’re still working to properly put a team together,” she said.

“We’ve got a bunch of amazing wheelchair athletes from lots of different sports. We’ve got Paralympians from basketball, wheelchair AFL, wheelchair rugby league, those similar sports.

“A lot of the team are trying to get up to speed with the skills of the sport and how it works. Meanwhile, I’m a little different.

“I know the ins and outs of handball and the strategy behind it, but I’m still learning how to best use a wheelchair. It’s all a huge learning curve for everyone.”

While the World Championships for 2026 are only a few weeks away, Brianna already has her eyes on a bigger event in 6 years.

“For a lot of us who play, we would love nothing more than to have wheelchair handball at the Brisbane Paralympics,” she said.

“I would like to see more exposure to the sport because every single time that someone sees a game or someone plays it or comes along to training, there’s always that response of why have I not played this before?

“It’s a really great blend of sort of all the sports that we really love in Australia. So I think that it really has the ability to grow and to grow really quickly, especially with Brisbane coming up as well.”

In the meantime, Canberra Handball is always on the lookout for new players.

“Canberra Handball has been doing a really good job at doing youth training,” she said.

“They’re doing youth training on Friday nights at Radford College, which is open to all, from junior to high school players and senior players as well.

“We would love to just see as many people get around the sport as possible.”

To follow Brianna, her trip to Spain for the World Championships and her push for representation at the 2032 Brisbane Paralympic Games, visit Wheelchair Handball Australia and Canberra Handball Club’s Instagram pages.

canberra.title: Canberra Short Film Festival moves into fourth decade with a new director calling the shots
canberra.snippet: The Canberra Short Film Festival is celebrating its 31st anniversary with its new director, Bruce Davie, who promises a huge lineup for 2...
canberra.content:
The Canberra Short Film Festival is celebrating its 31st birthday with a new director, Bruce Davie. Photo: Canberra Short Film Festival.

The Canberra Short Film Festival is celebrating its 31st anniversary with its new director, Bruce Davie, who promises a huge lineup for 2026.

The festival is one of the longest-running in the country. It has showcased some of the best short films ever captured, including last year’s International Best Film category winner, Berta.

This year’s festival received over 500 film submissions from across the world, with the best couple of hundred to be screened at Dendy Cinemas over the week-long festival (10 to 17 October 2026).

Mr Davie has been a long-time Canberra-based filmmaker and has served in other roles with the festival for years.

Replacing former director John Frohlich, Mr Davie said he is eager to give back to Canberra’s filmmaking community.

“John has been running the festival for 10 years, and he had it down to a sweet science, where he could run a very successful festival and do it quite comfortably,” he said.

“I’m still learning the ropes, but I’m lucky because I’ve been handed over a very mature festival with most of its systems in place. It’s just a matter of being able to execute.

“Personally, I’ve made over 20 short films over the years, and I believe that making films is a very demanding art form.

“You have to be part project manager, part artist, and you’ve got to pull a team together to execute a vision while also telling a compelling story in just a handful of minutes.

“Being able to support the current generation of filmmakers by being able to put their films on the big screen – that’s something I’ll always support.”

This year’s festival will continue the tradition of awarding the best films from around the world, with categories for Best International Film, Best National Film, and Best Canberra Film, along with awards for screenwriting, editing, and several other categories.

“Every year there are so many high-quality films belonging to so many different categories, whether that be comedy, drama, horror or whatever else. There’s so much experimentation and creativity on display,” Mr Davie said.

“Our judging panel are always blown away by the quality we see, not just by the international films but by locals as well.

“It’s rewarding not just for the filmmakers but for us as well to have their films shown in a dark cinema where people can be immersed. It’s one thing to see it on YouTube and another to be in a cinema where you can see if your jokes land or if the drama hits.

“Outside of festivals like the Canberra Short Film Festival, it’s really rare for people to have the opportunity to have their films shown like that.

“We at the festival are excited that we’ve been able to give people the opportunity to do that for 30 years and we want to continue doing that for many more years to come.”

The Canberra Short Film Festival will be held at Dendy Cinema from 10 October to 17 October. To purchase tickets or view the schedule for the festival, visit Canberra Short Film Festival.

australia.title: Sydney reaches 33C in potentially warmest start to spring since mid-1800s, while snow forecast in southern NSW
australia.snippet: A total fire ban is in place for greater Sydney with extreme fire danger exacerbated by hot and windy conditions Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Summer heat is due to arrive early across much of eastern Australia with potentially record early September temperatures predicted for Brisbane and Sydney, while snow was expected in southern New South Wales.

Maximum temperatures in Sydney during the first days of September were on track to match the city’s midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since the city’s Observatory Hill station opened in 1858.

Suburbs across Sydney were expected to reach up to 33C on Saturday afternoon, smashing average September records by up to 13C.

The temperature in Badgerys Creek reached 33C shortly before 2pm, while Observatory Hill hit 32.1C a short time later.

The meteorologist Tom Saunders said a gusty north-westerly airstream blowing south from the northern interior would lift maximums this weekend by as much as 13C above the average.

The highest anomalies were set to affect the NSW coast.

“For Sydney, it’s likely to be the hottest day this early in spring on record and for the first five days of September we’re on track to average a top of 27 degrees that matches the midsummer average,” he told ABC News.

“Temperatures this spring will average as much as three degrees above the baseline from recent decades, potentially the hottest spring on record.”

The warm, dry and windy conditions would cause fire dangers to spike. A total fire ban was in place for the greater Sydney region, where extreme fire danger was forecast.

The dramatic – and potentially dangerous – start to Australia’s spring extended across much of the continent, with damaging winds that could bring down trees and roofs in South Australia, and minor to moderate flooding for parts of Victoria and Tasmania.

Meanwhile, in southern NSW, live cameras appeared to show snow falling late on Saturday morning in Thredbo in the Snowy Mountains.

The Bureau of Meteorology had forecast snowfall to hit Thredbo top station by 4pm on Saturday, with a daytime low temperature of -1C.

The new falls won’t do much to help the parlous cover remaining on Australia’s ski fields after a warm winter, however.

The Weatherzone journalist Anthony Sharwood on Friday wrote: “September snowfalls are meaningful when there’s a decent remnant snowpack from winter onto which the new snow can bond. But … the Australian snowpack is at a historic low for the first week of September, even at the highest elevations of the mountains.”

Across the border, southern Queensland would see temperatures peak in the mid-30s in another unseasonably warm start to September.

In South Australia’s Mount Lofty and Flinders ranges, wind gusts of up to 110km/h were possible late Saturday into Sunday morning.

Heavy rains were forecast for north-east Victoria and northern Tasmania, with up to 60mm expected in some parts.

“The catchments in those areas are really wet,” the BoM meteorologist David Crock said on Friday. “They’ve seen multiple rounds of flood warnings this winter already.

“So we’ve got a flood watch current again for these catchments across northern Victoria … and across parts of northern Tasmania as well.”

The dramatic start to spring comes against the background of a “supersized” El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east, one that is already breaking heat records, and could comfortably surpass previous events.

On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.

El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.

Australia’s national council for fire and emergency services said fire authorities were predicting a heightened risk of fire across northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, parts of Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, and large parts of the Northern Territory.

australia.title: Rescue of Nepal hydropower workers ‘triumph for humans and humanity’, tunnelling expert says
australia.snippet: Arnold Dix, an Australian engineer and geologist who worked at Ground Zero after 9/11, says finding two workers alive in Trishuli 3A ‘giv...
australia.content:
There is renewed hope amid the devastation wreaked by the flash flooding disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border as the world witnesses “one of the great rescues of the 21st century”.

Nine days after the deadly floods, two workers were pulled out alive from a flooded hydropower tunnel in Nepal.

Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharajan were rescued from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project on Friday, more than a week after a glacial collapse created a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept away buildings, roads and bridges along the border between Nepal and China.

Hundreds more employees who worked in various hydropower projects along the banks of Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers remain missing, but the Australian engineer and geologist Arnold Dix, who was invited by Nepali authorities to advise on the Trishuli 3A operation, says Friday’s successful rescue will help lift spirits.

“We’ve found two people alive, so that gives us hope,” Dix says.

“After more than a week, everyone’s exhausted, but this spurs us on to try even harder and it now also gives us focus for how we might approach other rescues in other locations.

“We now have proof that people can survive this long.”

Dix has previously assisted at other disaster sites such as the 2023 Silkyara tunnel operation, where all 41 workers were rescued after a tunnel collapsed in India, and the tunnels of Ground Zero after 9/11.

But with almost 30 hydropower projects reported damaged, the Nepal floods are unlike any other disaster he has worked on.

“Normally, I deal with a single disaster – this is 27 concurrently,” he says.

On his specific rescue operation, workers had already had trouble identifying the location of Trishuli 3A. They then had to work out which tunnel would give access to the power station before the digging could begin.

But as the process began, rocks the size of vehicles blocked rescuers, forcing them to use explosives. This isn’t the preferred method, as it can pose risks to those on the other side, Dix says.

When they reached the tunnel, rescuers found it was full of water, forcing them to dig an emergency trench to try to drain it. They worried the workers inside could have already drowned, but on Friday morning about 50 metres in, they reported hearing a faint voice.

The team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you.” From inside the tunnel a voice replied: “OK.”

Watching the video of the men pulled from the tunnel alive reminds Dix of why he does this.

“We do it because we’re decent human beings and that’s what human beings do: help one another,” he says.

“This is a real triumph for humans and humanity.”

Another 40 workers are believed to be trapped inside Trishuli 3A and rescuers face significant risks. If there is water in the tunnel ahead of the team and they break rock, they could drown, and as they are now below flood-plain level, water could also inundate rescuers from behind.

“Yes, we have the reward of having rescued two people now, but we have to be so careful,” Dix says.

“The team’s lives are at risk right now and if they can’t get out in time they will drown.

“Like, this is not a drill, we are witnessing one of the great rescues of the 21st century.”

The rescue team was on Friday tunnelling to what is known as the “Goldilocks zone” at the top of the 11-storey Trishuli 3A power station, where they are hoping to find more survivors.

More than 270 people have already been rescued from various hydropower projects. At least 1,294 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency.

Thirty-eight Australian government officials, disaster response specialists and humanitarian workers are now on the ground in Nepal assisting in search-and-rescue and relief efforts. The latest cohort to arrive – a 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team providing specialist drone services – landed in Kathmandu late on Friday night. A further seven disaster victim identification specialists from the federal police will leave Australia on Saturday.

As at 4 September, the Nepali government has reported 1,294 confirmed deaths, while 5,053 people remain missing, including 583 foreign nationals.

As at 5 September, the Chinese government reported 31 confirmed deaths and 531 missing people, with 261 of those being foreign citizens.

Additional reporting by Ben Doherty

australia.title: Australia’s housing prices are trending down. See which suburbs have had the biggest falls
australia.snippet: Cotality says prices have declined in most capital cities over winter. Search the data to see how they have changed in your area Get our ...
australia.content:
Australia’s property market is facing a rare price correction, as rising interest rates and less favourable tax settings for investors accelerate a downturn.

Most capital cities recorded winter price falls, according to Cotality data, with Sydney leading the decline. That weakness is expected to continue, as higher inflation could lead to further interest rate hikes, denting demand.

But the recent price falls are not uniform.

In general, suburbs that previously recorded the biggest price increases also cooled the fastest. More affordable homes are also more likely to hold their value, given they are in demand by first home buyers aided by the government’s low-deposit scheme.

Those who have owned their properties for longer are also likely to be sitting on significant gains, even after the recent falls.

In some cities, including Brisbane, Perth and Darwin, home values are still up more than 10% over the past 12 months.

And the falls have not done much to make Australian homes more affordable for prospective homeowners, given rising mortgage repayment rates have cut borrowing capacity.

AMP notes that while home prices have fallen recently, “it’s just a flick off the top after a 50% surge since the pandemic”.

australia.title: ‘Sisyphus would be proud’: Queensland tribunal orders repairs to pool that doesn’t exist
australia.snippet: Tribunal immediately stays own order for repairs after noting that they were ‘impossible’ to carry out on the non-existent pool In an act...
australia.content:
In an act it compared to the ancient Greek myth of a man forced to roll a rock up a hill forever, a Queensland tribunal has ordered a company to make repair works on a pool that no longer exists.

It then stayed its own order, because the pool no longer exists.

Peter Roney KC, a member of the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal, handed down a judgment in the case this week.

“Sisyphus would be proud,” the judgment begins.

“I have been called upon to decide many outcomes in some strange and unusual circumstances whilst a member of this tribunal, but this case has its own special place,” Roney wrote.

The case was a challenge brought by the building firm Abel Gaspi Apolonia against what the tribunal said was an “almost incomprehensible” direction by the Queensland Building and Construction Commission relating to work done on a pool in Capalaba in 2021.

Part of the pool’s coping – a finish installed around the edges to stop leaking and prevent swimmers slipping – had had not been installed correctly and had sustained damage after heavy rain, the tribunal heard.

The coping work cost $300.

According to the judgment, the commission in 2024 directed the company that because “the installation of the copping (sic) has not been installed in an expected competent tradesman like manner” that “the non-structural defect falls Within 12 months of practical completion”.

But the tribunal said it was difficult to understand what work the commission wanted done and what the defect was.

The tribunal also said there was an even more fundamental problem: the pool had been removed in the meantime.

“After several hours of a hearing being conducted, using the resources of this state to determine what seemed to be an issue designed to protect a homeowner who had contracted for work on her pool, it was discovered, but only when the Commission checked, that the pool had ceased to exist for some years, and that the directive could not be given effect to in any way,” the judgment reads.

A lawyer acting for the QBCC submitted that the tribunal should still make a judgment, on the basis that it would be recorded on the builder’s licence history.

The tribunal handed down that judgment this week.

“To expect the resources of this state to be committed to making findings about the appropriateness of decision-making years earlier, in which has little or no practical significance, might be seen by many as a waste of public resources,” it reads.

“To decide the case anyway becomes an almost academic exercise. I will do so anyway. Sisyphus would be proud.”

The company argued that the pool was already old and defective before it was commissioned to work on it, that it made repairs that it had not been paid for and that the damage was caused by “excessive rainfall, soil movement, and the natural aging of the pool structure” rather than poor workmanship.

The tribunal ruled that the company had not repaired the coping as it said, and ordered that it rectify its work, but stayed its own order on the basis that it was impossible to carry out.

australia.title: A year after a deadly attack on two boys, Melbourne’s South Sudanese community remains in fear
australia.snippet: Victim’s father says community ‘struggling a lot’ as Victorian government yet to release report delivered eight months ago by expert grou...
australia.content:
On a Saturday evening last spring, two boys stepped off a bus in Melbourne’s outer west just before 8pm. They never made it home.

The alleged double murder of the two children – 12-year-old Chol Achiek and his friend 15-year-old Dau Akueng – reignited a fierce debate over solutions to curb Victoria’s youth gang violence.

The South Sudanese Australian boys were on their way home after a local basketball tournament when they were allegedly ambushed by a group of eight teenagers wielding machetes and knives on 6 September last year.

Victoria police charged the teenagers, aged between 15 and 19, with the murders of Dau and Chol the same month the pair were killed – there is no suggestion those charged are of South Sudanese background. The matter remains before the court.

At the time of the deaths the then Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, said solutions to fight against violent crime “must come from the community”. Offering her condolences to the boys’ families, Allan said she would convene a meeting of the government’s South Sudanese Australian Youth Justice Expert Working Group (SSAYJEWG) to hear solutions “first-hand”.

But a year on from their deaths the government is yet to release a report by the group – delivered more than eight months ago – which includes recommendations to improve community safety and reduce the over-representation of South Sudanese Australians in the youth justice system.

Guardian Australia understands the working group considered making a number of recommendations as part of its final report, including calling for Victoria police and other agencies to crack down on organised crime figures grooming African Australian children, and for the police force to publicly report stop and search data.

Other possible recommendations included pushing the Victorian government to increase early intervention programs in primary school, commission research on media reporting on young African Australians and work with the federal government to remove barriers faced by South Sudanese Australians in obtaining citizenship and accurate identification.

Dau’s father, Elbino Akueng, says a year on from the deaths, the South Sudanese Australian and Cobblebank communities are “struggling a lot”.

“It’s not just our family … it’s the entire community,” he says.

“There’s fear for [the] South Sudanese community.”

Akueng says he now drops off his two daughters, aged 8 and 12, at school because he does not want them walking the local streets alone. The pair used to walk to school with their older brother, Dau.

The working group was established in 2022 to help reduce the over-representation of South Sudanese Australian young people in Victoria’s youth justice system. While there is no suggestion Chol or Dau had interacted with the youth justice system, Allan last year pointed to the group – comprised of South Sudanese Australian leaders – as part of the solution to reducing street violence.

After the Cobblebank attack, the working group said its final report would provide the government with “systemic recommendations to create long-term positive change”.

“Preventing further tragedy requires us all to work together, such as families, elders, young people, service providers, community organisations, government and Victoria Police,” a statement from the group’s chair, Dr Santino Deng, and the deputy chair, Meena Singh, said.

“It is only through unity and collaboration that we can address the drivers of disadvantage and build pathways to safety, opportunity and success.”

In January, Deng posted on LinkedIn saying the group’s final report had been handed to the then youth justice minister, Enver Erdogan. Under new premier Ben Carroll’s cabinet reshuffle last month, Ros Spence now holds the portfolio.

A South Sudanese community leader, who requested anonymity to discuss the expert working group’s report, says there has been a “lot of work that has been put into this”.

“This is probably the most engagement we’ve ever had with the government,” the leader says.

“We just want to make sure that the government and community can continue to maintain the level of engagement that they have for the last few years and for the future as well.”

The leader says any allocated funding from the report’s recommendations should be provided to South Sudanese Australian community organisations to ensure they are involved in the reform’s implementation.

“If the government properly funds the recommendations of the expert working group I do believe that there can be a lot of work to prevent no further instances and help to stop our community being victims [of youth crime].”

A spokesperson for the Victorian government said its thoughts remain with Chol and Dau’s family, who were grieving after a tragedy that “should never have happened”.

“We stand with the community in their fight against youth gang crime. It’s why we are working with the South Sudanese Australian Youth Justice Expert Working Group to bring together local solutions,” the spokesperson said.

“We will continue to listen to the community, experts and Victoria police to understand what more can be done.”

The spokesperson did not respond to a question from Guardian Australia about what date the report would be published.

Brad Battin, the opposition’s spokesperson for police and corrections, said the premier – who has nominated tackling the root causes of crime as a top priority – had the ability to release the SSAYJEWG report as soon as possible.

“Waiting 12 months to see action to keep the community safe just sends more fear through the local community that they’re not being listened to,” he said.

Battin said the Coalition had committed $100m in crime prevention, to ensure that “we can get the programs that work out into these communities as fast as possible.”

The attacks on Dau and Chol occurred days after the state government’s machete ban amnesty came into effect, with members of the public urged to dispose of the long-bladed weapons in special amnesty bins installed at police stations across the state.

Last year, the government introduced tougher bail laws, adult time for violent crime” laws and created the violence reduction unit to respond to the “changed pattern of behaviour” by youth offenders.

The state’s latest crime data, for the 12 months to 31 March, showed alleged youth crime fell for the first time since 2022 but young people remained disproportionately represented in several serious and violent crime categories.

world.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
world.snippet: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has ...
world.content:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

world.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border Europe live – latest update...
world.content:
Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.

Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.

Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.

Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.

There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.

“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

world.title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation
world.snippet: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa The day dawned b...
world.content:
The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.

The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.

Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.

Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.

Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.

“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.

Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

world.title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
world.snippet: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have appr...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.

Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”

Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.

“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

world.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
world.snippet: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of t...
world.content:
Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.

The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.

Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.

The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.

The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.

Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.

“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.
